extracted.intended_audience: general public and legal professionals (law students, lawyers, policymakers)
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of the American Bar Association (ABA), describing its governance, law‑school accreditation standards and processes, ethics/model rules, and its judicial‑nominee rating procedures. Useful for readers seeking the ABA's substantive standards and procedural requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition as a law‑school accreditor
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States Department of Education recognises the Council of the ABA Section on Legal Education and Admissions to the Bar as a professional accrediting agency for law schools in the U.S.; ABA‑approved law schools are termed 'approved' by the ABA, indicating the law school was found to be in compliance with ABA accreditation standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ABA accreditation affects a graduate's ability to practice law in many U.S. jurisdictions: in most states graduation from an ABA‑accredited law school is a prerequisite to sit for that state's bar exam and often affects admission on motion to other states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard 509 — required public disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Law schools must disclose a wide set of information about applicants and graduates under ABA Standard 509 (the 'New ABA Standard 509').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required information now includes admissions data, tuition and fees, living costs, conditional scholarships, enrollment and demographic data, numbers of full‑time and non‑full‑time faculty, class sizes for first‑year and upper‑class courses, transfer data, attrition rates, employment outcomes and bar passage data. The Standard's purpose is transparency for prospective students and stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bar passage rate accreditation standard (75% rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: To remain ABA‑accredited, law schools must meet a bar passage threshold: the ABA changed its rule so that 75% bar passage rate must be achieved within 2 years (previously 5 years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The change (passed by the Section but with contested votes in the House of Delegates) has no exceptions and places schools failing the threshold at risk of sanctions, including potential loss of accreditation; proponents say it improves student preparation and reduces debt‑without‑employment risk, while opponents warn of adverse effects on diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissions testing requirement (LSAT or valid alternative)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Council voted (November 2022) to eliminate the accreditation requirement that law schools require prospective students submit LSAT results or an alternative valid and reliable standardized admissions test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the House of Delegates later rejected a proposal related to admissions, the Council in 2024 created a variance process permitting individual law schools to apply for permission to bypass the existing admission test requirement without House approval. The change has been debated over potential impacts on admissions objectivity and diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions for misrepresentation of employment/bar data
rubrics_metrics.description: ABA accreditation rules were updated (2011–2012) to include penalties and possible loss of accreditation for schools that misrepresent graduates' employment data and to greatly expand required reporting on bar‑passage rates and post‑graduate employment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These changes were intended to produce meaningful, accurate statistics for prospective students (responding to calls from groups like Law School Transparency); enforcement may include sanctions up to revocation of accreditation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard 206 — diversity and related accreditation expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA's Standards of Rules and Procedure for Approval of Law Schools includes diversity‑related requirements (referred to in the article as Standard 206), which the ABA uses in accreditation and approval processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard 206 has been the subject of legal and political scrutiny (e.g., claims by the U.S. Attorney General that it conflicts with Supreme Court decisions on affirmative action), and such disputes can implicate threats to the ABA's accreditation authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial nominee rating categories and evaluation process
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary evaluates prospective federal judicial nominees and rates them as 'well qualified', 'qualified', or 'not qualified'. The committee is composed of members drawn from the federal circuits and operates independently and confidentially.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations include review of legal writings, professional background, and judicial temperament; Supreme Court nominee evaluations involve added scrutiny (e.g., law‑professor teams reviewing writings). The committee notifies the White House, DOJ, Senate Judiciary Committee and the nominee of its rating. The process has been criticized for alleged ideological bias and has varied in whether it receives advance notice of nominees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethics rule prohibiting sexist, racist, condescending terms and age discrimination in bar activities
rubrics_metrics.description: In 2016 the ABA introduced an ethics rule prohibiting attorneys from using sexist, racist, and condescending terms, and from engaging in discrimination based on age in the conduct of bar association activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is part of the ABA's formulation of model ethical codes related to the legal profession; it applies to attorney conduct in ABA activities and reflects the ABA's role in setting professional standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antitrust/compliance obligations in accreditation
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA has legal obligations not to engage in anticompetitive conduct in its accreditation proceedings: in 1995 the DOJ accused the ABA of violating Section 1 of the Sherman Act; the matter was resolved with a consent decree, and a later acknowledgement (2006) of violating the decree resulted in a fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accrediting bodies must structure procedures to avoid unlawful anticompetitive restraints; prior DOJ action means the ABA's accreditation practices are subject to antitrust scrutiny and remedial obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governance and policy adoption procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA adopts organizational 'policy' positions via votes of its elected House of Delegates; the board of governors may act consistently with prior House action when the House is not in session. The Standing Committee on the Federal Judiciary is insulated from the House, board, and officers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding governance rules is relevant to how ABA standards and policies (including accreditation and ethics guidance) are created and updated; policies passed by the House or Section may be contested and can affect accreditation procedures and organizational stances.
